notes.1a: The majority of candidates correctly recalled the equation W = mg and calculated the weight of the balloon, stating the correct unit. Weaker candidates either omitted the units in the final answer or did not show their working as instructed or were unable to correctly recall the equation.
notes.1b: This ‘show that’ question required a correct equation to be quoted in any form and then the ratio 54/120 written down to gain credit. Weaker candidates correctly wrote down F = ma and then 54 = 120 × a without making acceleration the subject, so could not gain full credit.
notes.1c: Most candidates were able to recall the equation for acceleration and calculate the velocity by multiplying the acceleration by the time. Weaker candidates thought they needed to use velocity = distance/time, mistakenly dividing the acceleration value by the time.
notes.1d: The balloon did not have a constant velocity of 3.6 m/s so the majority of candidates did not realise they had to multiply the average velocity by 8.0s to calculate the correct answer. A few stronger �PAGE�41 0625 Physics June 2023 candidates sketched a velocity–time graph and found the area. A small minority of candidates correctly used equations of motion beyond the scope of the syllabus.
notes.2a: (i) The definition of pressure is in the Core column of the syllabus, but many students did not recall this correctly. Many said that force acted on an object but did not relate this to area. A common answer was to refer to “a certain area” rather than unit area. Simply quoting an equation even without the subject was sufficient for credit.
notes.2aii: Candidates who succeeded with this question had clearly learnt the equation for pressure at a depth. Weaker students often gained partial credit but thought that the pressure decreased with increasing density.
notes.2b: A considerable number of candidates thought that hydroelectric power and wind power were not derived from the Sun.
notes.2c: The majority of candidates answered both parts of this question well. They had many ways of explaining that supplies of nuclear fuel are finite and that power generation from waves in the sea is infinite.
notes.3a: (i) Candidates generally either got both (i) and (ii) correct or incorrect, suggesting that they knew the correct states of matter to select so they could compare the extremes of expansion but were unsure of the order.
notes.3aii: Stronger candidates who responded to the key words ‘motion and arrangement’, answered well. Many candidates stated that solid particles vibrate, are positioned in fixed or close positions and that gas particles move randomly. Weaker candidates did not refer to particles at all.
notes.3b: (i) In the definition required for this answer, it was necessary to refer to unit mass (since the word ‘specific’ refers to 1kg) and a unit temperature change. Weaker candidates incorrectly referred to molecules.
notes.3bii: Candidates demonstrated a good knowledge of the experiment to determine specific heat capacity. Weaker candidates did not recall that a temperature change requires measurement of the initial and final temperature.
notes.4a: (i) Candidates should be reminded that they should practice constructing the ray diagram using a sharp pencil and ruler for formation of a virtual image in the correct location. Weaker candidates displayed good knowledge of light-ray behaviour close to the principal axis but then tried to form a real image on the right-hand side of the lens.
notes.4aii: Candidates were often able to correctly identify the attributes of the image for an object located between the lens and the principal focus. Weaker candidates referred to their incorrect ray diagram to answer this question.
notes.4b: Many candidates correctly identified the defect of vision but were not confident about how this was corrected. Weaker candidates incorrectly mentioned use of a diverging lens or described the magnification properties of a converging lens as the means of correction.
notes.5a: (i) This question was only answered correctly by the strongest candidates.
notes.5aii: Generally, this question was not answered well. Candidates were not credited for statements such as ‘electromagnetic waves travel quickly’ or ‘undergo total internal reflection’. Correct answers needed to refer to the transparency to the radiation and also that high-speed broadband relies on the optical fibre carrying a high rate of data. �PAGE�42
notes.5b: (i) This question was generally answered very well. Weaker candidates often scored partial credit for a correct equation but if n = sini/sinr was used they did not realise that the sine of the critical angle should have been the denominator for light travelling from a denser to a rarer medium.
notes.5bii: This question demonstrated that total internal reflection was well understood but weaker candidates are advised to use a protractor in order to make the diagram look realistic with angles of incidence exceeding 45°.
notes.6a: Many candidates successfully selected and substituted into the correct electrical power equation from the Supplement column in the syllabus. Weaker candidates made an attempt to use P = IV by dividing the power by the resistance, believing this to be a voltage value. A very rare correct method was to use P = V2/R (beyond the scope of the syllabus) to find the voltage across the heater and then to calculate the current using P = IV.
notes.6b: This was a demanding question to which there was often no response, but stronger candidates gained full credit. Weaker candidates sometimes gained partial credit by evaluating the correct ratio of lengths and cross-sectional areas or by recalling the correct physics for the resistance of a conductor, e.g. resistance is directly proportional to length.
notes.6c: There were some good responses to this question. However, weaker candidates were unable to convert watts to kilowatts so consequently only partial credit was available.
notes.7a: This question was generally answered well. Weaker candidates arrived at a common incorrect answer of 46 A obtained by an incorrect recall of the relevant equation. Their correct ratio of voltages was equated to an incorrect and inverted ratio of the currents. Candidates should be reminded that since primary power = secondary power then V I = V I so equating ratios of p p s s voltages to currents does not follow the same pattern as the turns ratio equation.
notes.7b: This question was generally answered well. Weaker candidates sometimes gained partial credit by calculating the reciprocal of the correct answer.
notes.8a: (i) Only stronger candidates gave the correct answer. Weaker candidates stated that the neutron is ejected from the nucleus or that it is changed into either a proton or an electron.
notes.8aii: Only stronger candidates answered this correctly. Some other responses discussed energy conservation instead of charge. Some weaker candidates gained partial credit for stating that the neutron has no charge.
notes.8b: The majority of candidates knew how to complete a fully correct decay equation. Weaker candidates could not recall the numerical notation for the alpha particle or had a fully correct equation except they had substituted Rn for Po.
notes.9a: This question was very well answered and full credit could be awarded for Saturn and Jupiter placed correctly on the diagram. Partial credit was available for weaker candidates who calculated correct angles based on the ratio concept where the time of orbit represents 360°.
notes.9b: (i) The same technique as in (a) was required to answer this question. Stronger candidates realised that their calculation of 600° angular displacement of Jupiter equated to a full rotation plus a further 240° and this placed both planets 240° anticlockwise measured from S .
notes.9bii: This question was answered well. Weaker candidates thought the question was testing knowledge of the Earth’s orbit around the Sun, observing that it was in the same place after 20 years.
notes.9c: (i) The vast majority of candidates answered this question correctly. �PAGE�43
notes.9cii: When discussing density, most candidates found it straightforward to relate Jupiter’s low density to its gaseous composition. When discussing the gravitational field strength, stronger candidates were able to relate Jupiter’s large mass to its large value of gravitational field strength but weaker candidates just associated Jupiter’s large size with its large gravitational field strength.
notes.9d: The majority of candidates were able to correctly quote the density equation and then multiply density by volume. It proved difficult for most candidates to calculate the correct mass because they were unable to convert km3 to m3 where a multiplication factor of (1000)3 was required. Candidates are advised to refer to the mathematical requirements of the syllabus as they should be able to convert between metric units.
notes.10a: This question was generally very well answered, but some candidates did not recognise that for a ‘show that’ question the relevant equation needed to be included in addition to the necessary numerical steps.
notes.10b: (i) The majority of candidates answered this question incorrectly stating that direct measurements of either distance or time could be used to determine the speed of a galaxy.
notes.10bii: This question was only answered well by stronger candidates. Weaker candidates again assumed direct measurements were possible and often stated that speed = distance/time rather than recalling the equation involving the Hubble constant from the space physics section 6.2 (Stars and the Universe) of the syllabus.
notes.10iii: Although this was answered well by the strongest candidates, other candidates stated that direct measurements of speed and time were necessary. �PAGE�44
notes.key_messages:
• Candidates should take note of the command word and mark allocation of questions and should use
these details to ensure they answer appropriately.
• Numerical answers should be given to the required number of significant figures, with the correct
unit. Final answer (A) marks for calculations are only awarded for correct numerical answers with the
correct unit. Where either the numerical value is incorrect or the unit is missing or incorrect, marks
will only be awarded for working shown by candidates.
• Working for calculations should be set out logically, showing the formulae used.
• This syllabus now requires that candidates take the weight of 1.0kg to be 9.8N (acceleration of free
fall = 9.8m/s2).
• When asked to ‘show that’ a quantity has a particular value, candidates must demonstrate that they
know the formula they are applying. They should be advised to write down the formula in words or
notes.general_comments:
Many candidates had prepared well for this examination and demonstrated a good understanding across a
range of topics within the physics syllabus.
Manipulation of numbers given in the question to achieve the correct numerical answer is insufficient to
demonstrate understanding of the physics in the situation.
Candidates are expected to use the symbols for physical quantities given in the syllabus. Any alternative
symbol will only gain credit if it is clearly (and correctly) defined.
When candidates wish to alter their answer, they should cross out the response they do not wish to be
marked and write their new answer down (if necessary, using spare blank space in the answer booklet or a
continuation sheet and identifying the question number they are answering).
